playbook:
When a lot worth V to me comes up:
- Round 1: bid at or near the minimum raise only when V comfortably exceeds the minimum; otherwise pass.
- Round 2 (final): bid my full value V minus 1, because this is my last chance — bidding the bare minimum raise just gifts the lot to someone willing to top it. Accept that I may still lose: rivals do bid above my value sometimes (I lost lot 1 at 27 over value 24), and that is fine — I never chase past V−1.

Do not open weakly in round 1 expecting a round-2 comeback below value: another bidder will often jump above the minimum, and if the jump already prices out my surplus, I wasted nothing but lost the lot. Assume rivals bid aggressively on round 2.

Skip any lot where the standing bid is at or above my value; a bid equal to my value yields zero surplus, so I pass unless forced.

Track my budget exactly and conservatively: I KNOW my starting budget when it's stated (it was 30, not 100 — never invent a number), and I KNOW every lot I've won and what I paid. My remaining budget is start minus what I've actually paid for wins; losing bids cost nothing. My [budget] token must state that figure after deducting the bid I just made. If I truly cannot determine a number, I say what I do know ("no wins yet, so budget intact minus this bid") — I never guess a round number, never write "unknown" when the facts are knowable, and never contradict myself between turns.

Never bid more than my remaining budget. With a small budget (e.g. 30) and many lots, full-value round-2 bids can exceed it — cap my bid at budget, and remember budget only shrinks when I actually win.

On the last lot, only fight for it if its value exceeds the likely winning price by enough to beat my expected score from passing.

Reply ends with both tokens every time, even when I just pass.

1.text:
**Playbook for ref_auction**

- I report my actual remaining budget accurately. In this episode the opening screen stated a budget of 30 and I later claimed 100, which is indefensible. Before every reply I recompute: budget left = the *stated* starting budget minus only the bids I actually *won* (losing bids cost nothing; only the winning payment is deducted). I never invent or assume a starting number — I use the one given.
- If I am ever unsure of the starting budget mid-episode, I state the most conservative figure I can defend and I keep my bids safely under it, rather than guessing high.
- Money spent is a hard cap. I never bid more than my current remaining budget, and before a large bid I subtract what I still want for higher-value lots still to come.
- I pass when I am already the high bidder — I never raise myself. This worked (lot 3 won at 12 after passing).
- Early round: I bid the minimum raise to probe cheaply, but only when the minimum is well below my value.
- Final round is my last chance to win: if the minimum next bid is still clearly below my value, I bid decisively at or just under my value (as with lot 4 at 39) rather than adding a timid increment that still loses. In this episode timid small bids on lot 1 (25 vs rivals willing to pay 27) and lot 2 (17 vs 19) cost me profitable lots — when I want the lot, the final bid needs margin, not the bare minimum.
- One caution on final-round aggression: I never bid above my value, and I size the bid so win-or-lose the price is acceptable; a bid at exactly my value yields zero surplus, so when rivals seem to bid near my value I prefer passing and keeping the cash for better-surplus lots.
- I compare this lot's surplus (value minus likely price) against the surplus of remaining lots before committing a large bid, so I do not drain cash on a middling lot and lock myself out of a better one.
- I keep reasoning to one or two sentences, but I check the arithmetic twice: bid covers the minimum raise, bid ≤ my value, bid ≤ remaining budget, and the stated budget matches my ledger.
- I end every reply with the two bracketed tokens [bid: ...] and [budget: ...] as the last lines, with no trailing text.

2.text:
- Before anything else, I write down the starting budget exactly as stated in the episode intro (in this episode it was explicitly 30 — I later hallucinated a "standard 100" and reported figures like 73 and 54 that were pure invention). I subtract every winning bid the moment the result is announced and report only that tracked figure, never an assumed one.
- If my tracked budget and the game's shown state seem inconsistent, I trust the stated starting budget minus announced wins, and I say so briefly rather than silently switching to a guessed number.
- I treat my budget as a hard, scarce cap: I never bid more than I have, and before bidding on a marginal lot I check whether winning it would leave me unable to compete for a high-value lot still to come. In this episode I bid 27 on lot 1 against a stated budget of 30, nearly crippling myself for the remaining four lots — a 40-value lot and a 38-value lot came later. Spending almost everything on the first lot is a blunder even when the surplus is positive.
- Before bidding big early, I look at how many lots remain and reserve budget proportionally; with 5 lots I avoid committing more than roughly my fair share to any single early lot unless its value is extraordinary.
- When a lot's value to me exceeds the current standing bid plus the minimum raise, I bid the minimum raise needed to take the lead — never more. Pay-what-you-bid means every extra unit comes straight out of my score.
- When a lot's value is high and I have the budget, I still bid minimally rather than jumping toward my value; the goal is to win cheap, not to win convincingly.
- When the standing bid already meets or exceeds my value, I pass immediately (lot 4: standing 39 vs my value 21 — passing was correct). Raising there guarantees a loss no matter how cheap the minimum raise looks.
- When my value is near the standing bid but the required raise would push me over value, I pass.
- When my remaining budget cannot cover the minimum raise, I pass (lot 3 with 6 left) — and I treat that outcome as evidence I overspent earlier, not as bad luck.
- In round 1 of two, I bid only the minimum when interested; I save real decisions for round 2, since there is no benefit to establishing a large lead early — rivals can and do jump the price far past the estimate in round 2.
- I expect rivals to bid aggressively, sometimes above my value or the estimate; I do not interpret a low round-1 price as information about the final price.
- When deciding whether to chase a lot, I compare expected surplus (value minus likely price) against saving budget for later lots, and I only outbid others when the surplus stays clearly positive.
- I never let the brief reasoning replace arithmetic: each turn I compute value minus required bid and my remaining budget after winning before I type either token.
